Pre-light taste — a personal warning signal

You taste the wrapper before cutting and taste the cigar again afterward. When that pre-light taste is spicy, peppery or really strong, you often find you do not enjoy the cigar. This is your reported tendency, with exceptions—not an absolute rule.

How it affects predictions: Give a negative pre-light reaction meaningful weight when you report it for a particular cigar. It can lower confidence in a predicted match, but does not automatically justify an F. Your actual enjoyment or dislike while smoking takes priority. A mild or pleasant pre-light taste does not, by itself, establish an A or guarantee complexity.

Keep the evidence separate: Record this as perceived pre-light taste, not measured nicotine or a change to the published Strength category. Do not infer it from wrapper color, wrapper type or pepper notes in a review of the smoke, and do not assign it retrospectively as the reason for your three confirmed dislikes. Whether the post-cut taste is direct tobacco tasting or an unlit draw remains to be clarified.

Researched clues — hypotheses, not confirmed reasons

Scope: The comparison uses the original Honduran Punch Gran Puro and the original black-banded Obsidian. The latter is a provisional match for your name “Black Obsidian”; your exact release and both vitolas remain unconfirmed. Sources for Gran Puro Nicaragua and Obsidian White Noise have not been substituted.

Punch Gran Puro: Published notes include pepper, leather, dried fruit and cinnamon. Holt’s rates the line Medium–Full, while Cigar Aficionado rated the Santa Rita Medium. A separate historical Cigar Aficionado profile describes its wrapper and binder tobacco as nicotine-rich, without measured nicotine data. Hypothesis: tobacco intensity and/or its spicy character may explain your reaction better than plainness. Flavor profile · Holt’s classification · Santa Rita assessment · Historical blend profile

Original Obsidian: Cigars International rates it Full and describes espresso, pepper, earth, toast and cream; a staff review reports increasing body through the finish. Conversely, a CIGAR.com staff review reports little spice despite deceptive strength. Hypothesis: excessive or building intensity is more persuasive than a uniformly pepper-dominant or one-note profile. Profile and staff reviews · Contrasting first-hand review

Room101 Miami Snow: CIGAR.com classifies it Mild–Medium and describes cedar sweetness, nuts, cream and a little pepper; its staff tasting also characterizes the cigar as mellow and creamy. Published profile · CIGAR.com staff tasting. A separate first-hand review rates it Medium and describes bread, raw peanut and shell, cedar, then light green-pepper spice with little further change near the end. The reviewer nevertheless found it smooth and enjoyable. André Dias tasting, June 2025. Low-confidence possibilities: the particular woody/raw-nut/pepper balance or insufficient flavor development might not have suited you. A stable final third does not establish one-dimensionality. These reports do not support a specific high-nicotine explanation, nor do they rule out an individually uncomfortable experience. Cause remains unknown. Mildness and compatible flavor names are not enough to guarantee enjoyment; do not generalize this dislike to all Connecticut cigars or other Room101 blends.

Calibration: Your favorite Schizo Maduro also has a published Medium–Full profile with chocolate, spice, earth, pepper and wood. A shared note or strength category is therefore not sufficient for a rejection. C.L.E. description. Preserve your preference for manageable intensity over complexity, without treating flavor/body descriptions as nicotine measurements. All three dislikes stay confirmed F references; individual stock counts remain unrecorded, not zero.

Miami Snow calibration: This is a confirmed dislike with no remembered cause, despite a published mild-to-medium, creamy/nutty profile. Do not infer that every dislike comes from excessive strength, or that mildness plus favorable flavor names warrants an A. Assess the particular balance and credible complexity evidence. Your preference for manageable intensity over overpowering strength remains unchanged. No other blend is downgraded solely because it shares the Room101 brand, a Connecticut wrapper or a tasting note.

Enjoyable intensity first; complexity next. Your usual preference is layered flavor at a strength, pepper level and nicotine impact you enjoy. Excessive strength, dominant pepper or high nicotine that makes a cigar hard to finish is a larger mismatch than limited complexity. Between a plain but manageable cigar and an interesting but overpowering one, prefer the plain cigar. This is a relative enjoyment preference, not an instruction to finish a cigar or a statement about health risk.

Strength still varies with mood. Full cigars are rarely enjoyed and are an occasional exception, not an equally suitable default. Mild through Medium–Full may work when balanced; Medium–Full is not automatically rejected, and mildness alone does not earn an A. Grade your usual enjoyment, not only your most strength-tolerant mood. Rich flavor and complexity cannot compensate for a personally overwhelming experience.

Complexity is preferred, but secondary to intensity tolerance. Favor complementary layers, nuance and credible reports of development over a single dominant note. A mild or moderate one-dimensional cigar may be uninspiring, but that is a smaller drawback than being too strong to finish. Simplicity alone is not a reason for an F, nor does it automatically produce a D or E. Bitterness or harshness is a separate concern, not a synonym for simplicity. A stable profile can be layered; sparse descriptions do not prove simplicity, and a long tasting-note list or generic claim of complexity is not proof.

Flavor matching: cream, nuts, earth, leather, cedar, roast, coffee, cocoa/chocolate, vanilla and compatible sweetness are positive directions. Natural tobacco and infused profiles can both be excellent matches. Your enjoyment of Nub Nuance, Tabak Especial and Moontrance is not erased by your preference for complexity. A coffee-led or sweet cigar is not automatically simple.

Penalty priority: Give the largest negative weight to your direct reports of overwhelming strength, nicotine or pepper. Credible product-specific reports of these problems also lower predicted fit; flavor matches or complexity do not cancel a substantial intensity mismatch. Give a smaller penalty to a documented plain or one-note profile. Avoid inventing precise numeric weights from limited feedback. Spice as an accent is different from pepper dominating the smoke. Your earlier artificial/medicinal cherry dislike remains specific, not a rejection of all fruit or infused cigars.

Published Strength categories remain unchanged: Mild, Mild–Medium, Medium, Medium–Full and Full. Manufacturer “Mellow” wording is normalized to Mild. Published strength/body descriptions are qualitative and may disagree; they are not measured nicotine values. Pepper flavor, dark wrapper color, “Maduro,” full body and high nicotine are not treated as interchangeable evidence. A specific nicotine warning requires your experience or an explicit, credible report; it is not invented from a label.

A
Confirmed enjoyment, or an extremely strong predicted overall match with compatible flavors, supported balance and no substantial documented intensity mismatch. Complexity cannot cancel overpowering strength, nicotine or pepper. Predicted A is not a guarantee.
B
Likely to enjoy. A straightforward but compatible, manageable profile can rank here; limited complexity or a mild reservation does not automatically make it a poor fit.
C
Mixed or uncertain match. Can reflect limited depth, conflicting evidence, or unresolved intensity/pepper concerns. Read the rationale: a plain C is not equivalent to an overpowering C.
D
Unlikely to enjoy under usual preferences because a substantial documented mismatch dominates, particularly overpowering strength or pepper. Simplicity alone does not automatically warrant D.
E
Very unlikely to enjoy because multiple strong mismatches are documented, especially intolerable intensity plus dominant pepper or credible high-nicotine evidence.
F
Confirmed dislike from your direct feedback, not a claim that your tastes can never change. Punch Gran Puro, Black Obsidian and Room101 Miami Snow are F preference references. Full strength or limited complexity alone does not imply F.
Pending
The blend or release cannot yet be matched reliably. Not a low score.

Evidence priority: Your direct enjoyment or dislike takes precedence over published quality scores, marketing and speculative flavor matching. Keep confirmed favorites at A and confirmed dislikes at F. For Punch Gran Puro and Black Obsidian only, “possibly too strong” is an uncertain recollection. Room101 Miami Snow’s cause is unknown. Product-specific research may support labeled hypotheses, but must not convert an inferred cause into remembered experience or a confirmed nicotine, pepper or plainness problem. Avoid generalizing to entire brands or rejecting cigars solely because they share a flavor note. Conflicting sources reduce confidence. Construction, price and reputation do not determine the strength-and-flavor grade. Previously assigned inventory grades are unchanged by the addition of CAO Gold.

Reference profiles: Nub Single Roast; Nub Triple Roast; CAO Moontrance; Tabak Especial; CAO Eileen’s Dream. These support product descriptions; your feedback establishes enjoyment.

Preferences and stock are independent: You own some cigars you dislike. A favorite or a disliked cigar can be in stock; neither preference establishes possession or quantity. Punch Gran Puro, Black Obsidian and Room101 Miami Snow have no recorded quantities yet, which means unconfirmed—not zero or out of stock. Preference-only mentions of Single Roast, Double Roast, Tabak Especial, Moontrance and Schizo Maduro likewise do not establish stock counts. Record stock when identified or counted, regardless of grade, and never remove a stock entry merely because it is disliked.
